title: Hysterectomy | NHS inform
text:
Hysterectomy
A hysterectomy is the surgical procedure to remove the womb (uterus). After a hysterectomy, you’ll no longer have periods or be able to get pregnant.
A hysterectomy can be used as a treatment to manage health conditions such as:
fibroids
adenomyosis
prolapse of the uterus
cancer of the
uterus
,
ovaries
or
cervix
heavy periods
which are impacting your quality of life, other treatments have not worked and you do not want to get pregnant
If you are having a hysterectomy it’s important you’re prepared for surgery and know what it involves. It’s also important to know what to expect after surgery.
If you
have to wait for your surgery
, try to use the time positively and prepare yourself. For example by making changes to your lifestyle to support your health and wellbeing or getting some extra help and support with your mental wellbeing.
Types of hysterectomy
The most common procedure is a total hysterectomy. This is where both the womb and the cervix (neck of the womb) are removed.
There are other types of hysterectomy where:
only the womb is removed
the womb, cervix, fallopian tubes and ovaries are removed
the womb, fallopian tubes, part of the vagina, ovaries, lymph glands and fatty tissue are removed
The type of hysterectomy you have will depend on your circumstances. Your doctor will discuss your options with you and
you can ask any questions you may have
.
What happens during a hysterectomy
There are 3 ways a hysterectomy can be carried out.
The
types of anaesthetics
that can be used, how long you will be in hospital and the time you will need to recover will depend on which way your procedure is carried out. Recovery time will be around 6 to 8 weeks.
Laparoscopic hysterectomy
Laparoscopic surgery is also called keyhole surgery.
Keyhole surgery will usually be performed under
general anaesthetic
. The procedure might be carried out as a day case, meaning you don’t have to be admitted hospital, or you might be admitted to hospital overnight.
A small tube is inserted through a small cut in your stomach. This tube contains a telescope (laparoscope) and tiny video camera. This lets the surgeon see where they need to make further cuts to remove your womb and any other tissue, depending on the type of hysterectomy you are having.
Vaginal hysterectomy
A vaginal hysterectomy is when the womb and cervix are removed through a cut that’s made in the top of the vagina. This can be carried out under
general anaesthetic
or a spinal anaesthetic. Your doctor will discuss your options with you.
A vaginal hysterectomy is less invasive and recovery time is usually quicker. The procedure might be carried out as a day case, meaning you don’t have to be admitted hospital, or you might be admitted to hospital overnight.
Abdominal hysterectomy
An abdominal hysterectomy is when an incision will be made in your stomach (abdomen). You might need an abdominal hysterectomy if your womb is enlarged and is not able to be removed through your vagina.
General anaesthetic
is used for this procedure. To have this type of procedure you would usually be admitted to hospital for 2 to 3 days.
Risks and benefits
Having surgery may help treat, or in some cases cure, symptoms that you have been struggling with. You’ll no longer have periods or be able to get pregnant.
Having any type of surgery, or general anaesthetic can have risks particularly if you:
have other illnesses
smoke
are overweight
Your doctor will discuss the risks and benefits with you to help you decide what’s right for you.
You can ask any questions you might have.
Recovering from a hysterectomy
Straight after surgery, it’s normal to feel tired and have some pain. You’ll be given pain medication to help ease the pain.
You’ll have a dressing or dressings placed over your wounds to help them heal and keep them clean. You’ll be given advice on how to care for your wounds. Your doctor or nurse will also explain what things you can do and what things you should try to avoid while recovering. For example:
when you can do gentle exercise
when you’re able to drive
when you’re able to go back to work
when you’re able to have sex
It usually takes between 6 to 8 weeks to recover from this type of surgery, however for some people it may take longer before they feel fully recovered. You can contact your GP practice to discuss any concerns about your recovery.
After a hysterectomy, some people might find they have feelings of loss, sadness or find it difficult to come to terms with no longer being able to get pregnant.
You should talk to your GP if you experience low mood that won’t go away. Support is available.
Further information about your mental wellbeing
Menopause
After having a hysterectomy, you’ll no longer have periods. If you had your ovaries removed during your surgery, you will experience the menopause.
All women will experience the
menopause
differently, but there are some common symptoms that are helpful to look out for:
Some of the symptoms of menopause include:
hot flushes
mood changes
fatigue
difficulty sleeping
joint aches
vaginal dryness or pain
There are a lot of things that can help
manage symptoms of menopause
.
You can also speak to someone at your GP practice about your symptoms and ask if they’re related to menopause. You can ask to see a female health professional, if you prefer.
Menopause symptom questionnaire
You can use our
menopause symptom questionnaire (PDF, 168KB)
to keep a note of your symptoms and how you’re feeling. You can print it and talk about it with your healthcare professional to help them understand the different symptoms you’re experiencing.
